To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the pH rise during degradation of bioactive glasses is reduced by the addition of fluoride, but that fluorapatite formation is favoured by an increase in the phosphate content of the glass.

the formation of fluorapatitic carbonated hydroxyapitite is promoted by the presence of fluoride and phosphate in bioactive glasses and that the formation of apatitic phases is favoured by an increased phosphate content in the bioactive glass.

(i) incorporation of fluoride in bioactive glasses reduces the pH increase during dissolution and formation of apatites in SBF, but (ii) increasing fluoride content in glasses results in formation of fluorite at the expense of fluorapatite.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the effect of glass composition and structure on the properties of bioactive glasses, in particular fluoride-releasing glasses.
the development of fluoride-releasing bioactivity and the influence of glass composition and structure on the degradation behaviour and formation of apatites in body fluids.
the effect of glass design (i.e. composition and structure) on the formation of FAp and the release of fluoride in SBF.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

fluoride-containing glasses with higher phosphate contents, but lower fluoride contents, would be most suitable for dental applications, while glasses with higher fluoride content would be more suitable for orthopaedic applications.

the formation of FAp is not only dependent on the fluoride content of the glass but also on the phosphate and calcium content of the glass, as these components are released into the surrounding solution.

the glass structure and composition, in particular, fluoride content, phosphate content and calcium/phosphate ratio, have a strong effect on pH, ion release, and apatite phase formation in SBF, and these factors need to be taken into account when designing fluoride-containing bioactive glass compositions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

fluoride-releasing bioactivity of the glasses is dependent on the glass composition and structure and that a balance between phosphate and fluoride in the glass needs to be achieved to obtain optimal fluoride release, pH and apatie formation in SBF.
fluoride release from the glass is the most critical aspect for formation of FAp in body fluids, whereas the glass structure and composition have only minor effects on the pH and ion release.

the design and structure of fluoride-containing bioactive glasses can be optimized to control pH, ion release and the formation of FAp, with the potential to enhance the performance of these materials for orthopaedic and dental applications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of fluoride-containing glasses for dental applications should take into account the formation of fluorite, which can reduce the bioactivity of the glass.
fluoride-containing bioactive glasses can be tailored to release fluoride and form FAp, which is more chemical stable than hydroxy- or carbonated hydroxylapatite.
the formation of FAp in SBF is a function of both the composition and the structure of the bioactive glass.
